one_liner: Low-RAM, no-malloc animated GIF decoder for MCUs and PCs; claims to beat giflib but publishes no comparison.
what_it_does: Decodes animated GIFs from RAM, flash, SD card or any callback-backed source and hands you one scan line at a time through a GIFDraw callback, so a 24-32K RAM microcontroller can stream frames to an SPI LCD without holding the canvas. With a caller-supplied frame buffer it can also composite frames and emit 'COOKED' RGB565/RGB888/RGBA8888 or 1-bpp pixels. The API is an Arduino-style C++ class (open/playFrame/close plus setFrameBuf/setTurboBuf) over a C99 core that also exposes GIF_* C functions; it is not giflib's DGif API.
how_it_is_fast: Normal mode is a classic linked-list LZW decoder tuned for MCUs: the chunked LZW stream is first 'de-chunked' into a flat buffer, codes are pulled from a 32- or 64-bit bit-buffer, and runs are copied with word-sized unaligned stores where the CPU allows it. Turbo mode (DecodeLZWTurbo) uses the output image itself as the LZW dictionary: each code is stored as an (offset, length) pair into already-decoded pixels, so emitting a string is a forward memcpy instead of a backwards linked-list walk and reversal. Recent commits add ESP32-S3/P4 assembly (s3_transparent.S, p4_transparent.S) and Arm NEON paths for transparent-pixel merging and palette lookup.
when_to_use: Playing GIF animations on microcontrollers (ESP32, Cortex-M0+/M4/M7, ESP8266, RP2040-class) where you cannot afford a full frame buffer or any malloc.
Streaming decoded lines straight to an SPI LCD (optionally via DMA) while the next line decodes.
Small embedded GUIs that play your own pre-made GIF assets from flash, where the images are known-good.
Desktop or Raspberry Pi tools that want a dependency-free single-source GIF player and can live with the 2048-pixel width cap under __LINUX__.
when_not_to_use: Decoding untrusted GIFs: two buffer-overflow reports are open and unanswered (#115, 2026-01-27; #117, 2026-02-17, unvalidated LZW minimum code size), and the current source still reads ucCodeStart without checking it is 2-8.

Turbo mode on any input you do not control: DecodeLZWTurbo never checks that a code is already defined and its copy routine has no bounds check by design (source comment: a check 'slows everything down about 10%'), and the repo's fuzz tests never enable Turbo.
Wide images: canvas width is capped at 480 pixels on non-Linux builds and 2048 with __LINUX__ defined (GIF_TOO_WIDE otherwise).
When you need a measured win over giflib on a PC: no number against giflib exists in the repo; use gif_load or giflib-turbo instead.

Animations that rely on disposal method 2 or local palettes in low-RAM modes: the README warns they render incorrectly without a full canvas, and Turbo mode skips the previous-frame disposal restore that DecodeLZW performs.

integration.dependencies: none (libc string functions; Arduino.h when built for Arduino). Examples additionally use display libraries such as bb_spi_lcd or TFT_eSPI.
integration.min_toolchain: C99 for the core (gif.inl); C++11 for the class wrapper (uses nullptr). linux/Makefile builds a static libAnimatedGIF.a with -O2.
integration.platforms: Any MCU with roughly 24-32K free RAM (Arduino 'architectures=*'), plus Linux/macOS desktops and Raspberry Pi; optional NEON on Arm and assembly SIMD on ESP32-S3/P4.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; all decoder state lives in the per-instance GIFIMAGE struct (about 25 KB, embedded in the class), so separate instances on separate threads should be independent.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces giflib functionally for playback, but with a different callback-based API; giflib-turbo (same author) is the API-compatible drop-in.

gotchas: Turbo RAW mode never calls GIFDraw: pixels are left in the turbo buffer (frame-sized, not composited), so you either read getTurboBuf() yourself or use COOKED with a frame buffer; issue #111 (open) reports COOKED Turbo output is wrong when no draw callback is given, and the code path assumes 16-bit output there.

RAM figures disagree: README says Turbo needs 'another 32K', the header says '48K + full framebuffer', and allocTurboBuf actually allocates TURBO_BUFFER_SIZE (24,832 bytes) plus canvas width x height with plain malloc (uninitialized).

On every 64-bit target ALLOWS_UNALIGNED is forced and the code type-puns unaligned 8-byte loads and stores, and Turbo mode fills the ucLZW array past its declared size into the following struct members (usGIFTable, ucGIFPixels, ucLineBuf); this works on x86-64/AArch64 but is undefined behavior that sanitizers will flag. A 64-bit pixel-overwrite bug (#112) was fixed only in November 2025.
ESP32/ESP8266 users playing GIFs from RAM must supply their own file callbacks, because the in-memory reader assumes flash and uses memcpy_P.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick AnimatedGIF over gif_load or giflib-turbo when the target is a microcontroller driving an LCD line by line with no heap; on a PC, gif_load has published timings against giflib 5.2.2 (1.28x-1.78x) and giflib-turbo keeps giflib's API with the same Turbo LZW technique.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing compares this library with giflib or any other decoder: perf.png only times one 8-frame 160x120 GIF (badgers.h) across six MCU boards (Cortex-M7 600 MHz 8,134 us to Cortex-M0+ 48 MHz 357,160 us) without naming the mode or library version, and the 2-30x figure is Turbo against the library's own Normal mode with no table. The only harness, examples/gif_benchmark/gif_benchmark.ino, is not like-for-like: its Turbo arm decodes RAW pixels with no palette conversion or draw callbacks, while its Normal arm runs COOKED RGB565 conversion plus a per-line callback, so its 'nearly 2X' overstates the decoder difference. A first-party 2021 blog post on the 'big memory' decoder (blocked here; search snippet only) claims about 5x faster than giflib on poorly compressed images and over 20x on well-compressed ones, with no harness.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-07-03, v2.2.3 in library.properties, frequent 2025-2026 fixes and SIMD additions) and Apache-2.0, so it is easy to vendor, but two security reports have sat open for months, so treat it as a decoder for trusted assets only.
